hints.junior: A five-year-old app can hit 340 violations on the first axe run — fail-on-any-violation blocks every unrelated PR until someone disables the check.
hints.mid: 'Fail on any violation' conflates 'does this app have a11y problems' with 'did this change make anything worse' — a check that can't tell those apart gets disabled, not fixed.
hints.staff: Same failure shape as any retroactively-introduced linter on a large codebase — a check that starts red on day one and can't isolate new regressions gets turned off.

hints.junior: Click 'Run axe in CI' in each mode — the page has the same 3 pre-existing violations both times, watch how each policy handles them.
hints.mid: Try 'Simulate new violation' in baseline mode afterward — it shows the check still catches a real regression instead of just going green forever.
hints.staff: The baseline is keyed by rule id plus CSS selector, not just the rule id — that's what lets it catch a new contrast failure on a different element while ignoring the tracked one.

hints.junior: Run axe once, save what it finds as a baseline. From then on, only a violation NOT in that baseline fails the build — known issues stay tracked but don't block unrelated work.
hints.mid: Each baseline entry is a rule id plus the CSS selector from that violation's node.target — fixing one instance of color-contrast doesn't un-baseline every other instance of that rule.
hints.staff: This is deliberately not axe.configure disabling a rule outright — that turns the rule off everywhere including brand-new code, where the baseline only allowlists specific already-known pairs.

hints.junior: Don't disable a whole rule to quiet a noisy page — that hides new violations of that same rule too. Allowlist the specific known instances instead.
hints.mid: Scan a stable DOM state (after loading/animation settles) and use context.exclude for third-party subtrees you don't control, rather than disabling the rules they happen to trigger sitewide.
hints.staff: Track the baseline's entry count on a dashboard and require a linked ticket for any addition — without that discipline it decays into the same 'everything's allowed' state as the disabled check it replaced, just more quietly.

sections.junior: Today's case is about running axe-core in CI, and why the obvious first setup, fail the build on any violation, gets disabled within a week on a real codebase with any accessibility debt at all.
sections.mid: Fail on any violation conflates two questions — does this codebase have accessibility problems, and did this specific change make anything worse. A check that can't tell those apart gets disabled or configured so loosely it stops catching real regressions.
sections.staff: This is the same shape as any linter introduced retroactively onto a large codebase — a check that starts red on day one and can't distinguish pre-existing debt from new regressions gets disabled, not fixed.

sections.junior: The fix is a baseline. Run axe once, save what it finds as known issues, and from then on only fail the build on a violation that isn't already in that baseline.
sections.mid: A baseline entry is the rule id plus the CSS selector, not just the rule id alone, so fixing one instance of a violation doesn't accidentally un-baseline every other instance of that same rule elsewhere on the page.
sections.staff: This is deliberately not the same as disabling a rule entirely — that turns it off everywhere, including new code the PR adds, so a brand-new failure would pass silently. The baseline only allowlists specific, already-known pairs.

sections.junior: Try running axe in CI under each policy, and then simulate a new violation in baseline mode to see it still gets caught.
sections.mid: In baseline mode, simulating a new violation adds one that isn't in the baseline and reruns the check — it still catches the regression instead of just going green forever.
sections.staff: The baseline is keyed by rule id plus selector, not just the rule id — that's what lets it catch a brand-new failure on a different element while still ignoring the tracked one.

sections.junior: Fail on any violation gets disabled fast. Baseline the known issues, fail only on new ones, and track the baseline size so it shrinks instead of growing quietly.
sections.mid: Record a baseline of known violations, then diff future runs against it — fail CI only on violations a PR actually introduces.
sections.staff: Allowlist specific instances, not whole rules, and track the baseline's size on a dashboard so it burns down instead of quietly growing.
